newsitem.title: USA: Dlr ends nearly flat to weaker in US, eyes assets.
newsitem.headline: Dlr ends nearly flat to weaker in US, eyes assets.

text.p: The dollar ended nearly unchanged against the yen and weaker versus the mark after a late sell-off in U.S. stocks and bonds pressured the greenback, currency experts said.

"The pressure ... at the end of the day is primarily due to what seems to have been the sudden correction in the direction of the bond market and the stock market after what should have been an uneventful end of the FOMC meeting," said Hillel Waxman, a first vice president at Bank Leumi Trust Co of New York.
The Federal Open Market Committee, or FOMC, the Federal Reserve's policy arm, voted on Wednesday to leave short-term interest rates unchanged, as expected by most economists.

But stocks ended sharply lower after a sell-off in technology shares spilled over into the broader market. The Dow Jones industrial average finished down about 86.58 points at 6,746.90. Meanwhile, the price of the 30-year U.S. Treasury bond fell more than a half point.
The dollar closed at 123.35/45 yen, barely higher than 123.32/42 yen at the open. It fell to 1.6445/55 marks from 1.6495/00 marks.

Earlier in the day, the dollar scored a new four-year high of 123.85 yen, extending a rally that had begun overnight as the Japanese stock market sold off sharply amid rumors that Nippon Credit Bank Ltd was having financial difficulties.
Nippon Credit later denied it was having trouble raising funds and said rumors it could collapse were groundless.
Helping fuel the dollar rally were the British pound's sharp gains on the yen, which some analysts linked to issuance of corporate bonds denominated in both yen and pounds.
The British currency surged above 202 yen for the first time in more than four years.
Japanese investors are keen to buy pounds or sterling and other higher yielding overseas assets because interest rates in Japan remain at rockbottom levels.
"People are nervous about financial institutions in Japan," said Jeffrey Yu, a senior dealer at Sanwa Bank Ltd in New York.

"But at the same time, the other concern in the Japanese domestic market is individuals are divesting from the Japanese domestic market and investing overseas," Yu said. "That's why sterling is also rising."
Brian McCarthy, a market analyst at Ruesch International, said, "The dollar's gains against the yen are an indirect result of sterling's gains against the yen, at least today."
Initially, the dollar had strengthened against the mark after a government report indicated that the German economy was still struggling to recover.
West German industrial orders fell 1.4 percent in December and offset a 0.2 percent rise in east German orders.
"It says the German recovery is not preceding as quickly as had been hoped," McCarthy said. "That helped the dollar out overnight."

Yet by the close of trading in New York, the dollar was lower against the mark and had nearly erased all of its gains versus the yen. Traders attributed this partly to the late decline in stocks and bonds.
Elsewhere, the dollar finished at 1.4235/45 Swiss francs, down from 1.4303/08 francs at the open. Sterling rose to $1.6430/40 from $1.6298/08.
The dollar ended at Canadian $1.3445/50, up slightly from C$1.3434/39. The Australian dollar finished at $0.7630/35, up from $0.7611/16 at the open.
